title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:52Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank point covers Aboriginal rights and discrimination broadly and mentions the Tent Embassy only as one item in a list, so it is broader than the new point, which is about the Tent Embassy itself as a lasting symbol of land-rights protest.

draft.title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
card: On 26 January 1972, four Aboriginal activists put up a beach umbrella and then a tent on the lawn opposite Parliament House in Canberra. They were Michael Anderson, Billy Craigie, Bertie Williams and Tony Coorey.

They wanted land rights: legal recognition of Aboriginal peoples' connection to their land. They were also protesting against the government's recent statement that it would not recognise land rights, and offered only leases on some land.
They called it an embassy to make a point. Aboriginal people felt like foreigners in their own country, with no say in the decisions made about their land.

Police removed the tents in July 1972, but the protest drew thousands of supporters and was re-established. The Tent Embassy has stayed on the site in various forms, and it is still a symbol of Aboriginal protest and the push for land rights.
draft.remember: A tent on the lawn of Parliament House turned a protest for land rights into a lasting symbol.

a.q: Why did the activists name their protest an embassy?
opts: To show Aboriginal people were treated as foreigners at home
To claim Canberra as a separate country with its own laws
To ask other nations to send diplomats to Australia
To show they had been invited by Parliament to speak
a.why: An embassy belongs to a foreign people, so the name pointed to Aboriginal people having no say in their own land. The protesters did not claim to be a separate country. They were demanding recognition and land rights within Australia.
a.clue: Think about who normally has an embassy in a capital city.

b.q: Why is the Tent Embassy still seen as important today?
opts: It became a lasting symbol of protest for land rights
It was the first place where land was handed back
It was built by Parliament to host Aboriginal leaders
It ended all protest because land rights were then won
b.why: The Embassy was set up in 1972 and has remained on the site in various forms, so it stands as a symbol of protest. It was a protest site, not a land handback, and it did not end the campaign for land rights.
b.clue: Think about what a tent on the lawn of Parliament House stands for.

a.best: To show Aboriginal people were treated as foreigners at home

b.best: It became a lasting symbol of protest for land rights

problems.detail: 'Parliament House' in 1972 was the building now called Old Parliament House. Today's students may think the Embassy is at the current Parliament House. Say 'opposite what is now Old Parliament House'.
'Has stayed on the site in various forms' suggests it was there without a break. It was removed and re-established several times and has been continuously on the site only since 1992.

check.summary: Facts and both questions check out, and each question has one clear right answer. Two small card fixes are needed: make clear it is opposite what is now Old Parliament House, and note that the Embassy was not on the site continuously until 1992.

proposal.title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
card: On 26 January 1972, four Aboriginal activists put up a beach umbrella and then a tent on the lawn opposite what is now Old Parliament House in Canberra. They were Michael Anderson, Billy Craigie, Bertie Williams and Tony Coorey.

b.q: Liam visits Canberra and sees the Tent Embassy opposite Old Parliament House. Which statement about its history is accurate?
opts: It was removed several times and has stayed since 1992
It has stood on the site without a break since 1972
It was set up to celebrate land rights won in 1972
It was first set up in 1992 to mark a land rights win
b.why: The Embassy began in 1972, was removed and set up again several times, and has stood there without a break only since 1992. It is tempting to think it has been there nonstop since 1972, but police removed it that same year. It was a protest against the refusal of land rights, not a celebration.
b.clue: Did the tents stay put after police arrived in July 1972?
